newsitem.title: UK: Britain braced for fourth interest rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Britain braced for fourth interest rate rise.

text.p: Britain's official 6.75 percent interest rates are likely to rise for the fourth month in a row on Thursday when the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee finishes its two-day monthly meeting, analysts said on Tuesday.

The decision is a tough one, given the widening split between the rampant consumer and service sector and subdued manufacturing industry, already cowering in the face of the pound's persistent strength.

But on balance a rise to 7.0 percent is probable as the central bank tries to make sure the current mini-boom does not culminate in a bust. A survey by Reuters showed 16 out of 23 economists expected rates to rise on Thursday. (The Bank will announce its decision at 1100 GMT on Thursday.

Industrial production data released on Tuesday underlined the dilemma confronting the monetary authorities. Overall industrial production grew by 1.4 percent in June, well above expectations of a 0.5 percent increase, but most of the gain came from the energy sector which increased its output due to poor weather in the second half of June.
Manufacturing output improved by just 0.4 percent in June, recouping less than half May's 1.0 percent drop.

"These figures make a close call on interest rates even closer," said HSBC UK economist Jonathan Loynes. "But with the committee concentrating on the strength of services, a further rise in interest rates is probably still the most likely outcome."

There are fears that another rise in interest rates, which have risen from 6.0 percent since May, could push the pound to new heights. It rose two pfennigs on Tuesday and was up at 3.0533 marks, edging back towards the decade high of 3.0878 set last month.

The Office for National Statistics said there was "no obvious effect" from the strength of the pound on the June output data and argued that manufacturing output was still high even if it was down from its peak.

But a Confederation of British Industry (CBI) survey showed that export optimism had plummeted in 10 out of the 11 UK regions. It blamed the rise in the average value of sterling to 2.91 marks in the four months to July, from an average of 2.75 in the April survey.

However, there were some signs that the recent rises in interest rates might actually be starting to bite into demand and helping to check the inflationary potential of the 35 billion stg in free shares handed out to British consumers by building societies which are turning into banks.

Tuesday's UK purchasing managers' (PMI) monthly survey of the services sector showed a slight moderation in the pace of growth. The survey, sponsored by Reuters, showed the first signs that the strong pound was also beginning to hurt service firms.

"It is difficult to infer too much from a survey with such a short history, but the lower readings...suggest that the effects of policy tightening are already feeding through," said NatWest Markets UK economist John O'Sullivan.

He argues that a rate rise this week will be the last for a year. "Once they've raised rates this week they can sit back and assess the data and they'll be able to say in the inflation report that they're on course to hit the inflation target," he said.
The Bank of England is due to publish its quarterly Inflation Report, in which it assesses the chances of hitting the official 2.5 percent inflation target two years ahead, on August 13.
CIBC chief economist David Coleman said the PMI survey showed trade in services was not immune to the strong pound.
"If this survey does indeed herald the start of a period of more subdued growth in services, then some of the more pessimistic forecasts for UK interest rates could well prove misplaced," he said.

Forecasts for the peak in UK rates range from 7.0 percent up to one economist's forecast of 8.25 percent, according to the Reuter survey. The mode is 7.5 percent, predicted by nine economists, but 8.0 percent is the next most popular forecast, suggested by six of those surveyed.

The three-month interest rate futures contract on the London International Financial Futures Exchange, a key guide to interest rate sentiment, suggests the peak will be 7.25 or 7.5 percent and will be reached by the end of the year, although it is then discounting almost no movement in rates until the end of the century.
